title: Graphs
text:
One of the major issues with a decentralized system for tracking property data is that each county has their own system for tracking and storing data. This includes both what data they store as well as the variable names and format that they choose to store it in. As such, most of this analysis will be on individual counties.
















Aitkin county reports both land area as well as zoning code for each of their parcels. From this we can see that unsurprisingly the most common zoning is residential however it comes 6th in total area. Rural vacant land (no houses or farmland) is both high in area and number of parcels likely due to large forested areas owned by many different people.
















Ramsey County, being the biggest in our dataset, contains many different suburbs that we can look at. Comparing cost of property to count of property we see that the most populated areas: Saint Paul and Maplewood are on the lower side of property values while the less populated suburbs are on the higher side. Interestingly, Arden Hills shows the highest gap between median and average cost of property indicated a high density of inexpensive property offset by a lesser amount of dispproportionally expensive properties.









Sorting counties by average parcel size gives us an idea about how urban or rural a county is. Counties like hennepin and ramsey which contain very densly populated areas have a much lower average area than counties like beltrami or bigstone which are much more rural.

title: Tracking Land Ownership Changes in Minnesota
text:
Our project examines how land ownership in Minnesota has changed over time using parcel-level data from the Minnesota Geospatial Information Office (MnGeo).We analyze variables such as parcel size, owner, land type, assessed value, and property taxes to understand patterns in ownership transfers, land use, and differences between private and public ownership.
Research Question: How has the rate of land ownership transfers in Minnesota changed over time?
Data Source: Minnesota Geospatial Information Office

title: SDS 264 Project
text:
Project Overview

This project examines how land ownership patterns in Minnesota have changed over time using parcel-level data from the Minnesota Geospatial Information Office. Our primary goal is to analyze the rate at which land parcels transfer from one owner to another and to identify trends in ownership among individuals, corporations, and government entities. By studying these changes, we aim to better understand how land ownership influences economic development, land use, taxation, and environmental management across the state.
The dataset includes detailed information on parcel size, ownership, location, district, land type, assessed value, and property taxes. We are also working to incorporate a year variable so that ownership changes can be tracked over time. Using R, web scraping techniques, and geospatial visualization tools such as Quarto and Leaflet, we create interactive maps and charts that allow users to explore land ownership patterns throughout Minnesota. This project was developed as part of a data science course at St. Olaf College and demonstrates how data science can be used to answer important questions about land ownership and resource management.
